ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All participants provided written informed consent.

> Specifically, participants were asked: "Has a doctor ever told you that you have been diagnosed with a heart disease (including myocardial infarction, coronary heart disease, angina, congestive heart failure, or other heart problems)?"

> A total of 4,823 participants were included in this analysis, drawn from the HRS cohort (N = 3,258) and the ELSA cohort (N = 1,565).

> All procedures performed in studies involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and national research committees and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards.

> (40) Participants were eligible for inclusion if they: (1) were aged ≥45 years at baseline; (2) had no prevalent CVD prior to the end of the exposure ascertainment period; (3) had complete data

> All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.

> The HRS was approved by the University of Michigan Health Sciences and Behavioral Sciences Institutional Review Board (Protocol No.

> ELSA received ethical approval from the relevant UK Research Ethics Committees across waves (Wave 2: ) eGDR (mg/kg/min)=21.158-(0.09×WC)-(3.407×HT)-(0.551×HbA1c) where WC denotes waist circumference (cm), HT represents hypertension status (1 = yes,0 = no), and HbA1c indicates glycated haemoglobin (%).

> Health and Retirement Study was approved by the University of Michigan Health Sciences and Behavioral Sciences Institutional Review Board (Protocol No.

> The English Longitudinal Study of Ageing received ethical approval from the relevant UK Research Ethics Committees across waves (Wave 2: MREC/04/2/006; Wave 4: 07/H0716/48; Wave 6: 11/SC/0374).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.header: Independent Contributions of Trajectory Class and Cumulative Average eGDR
table.expanded: In HRS, cumulative average eGDR was no longer associated with incident CVD after adjustment for trajectory class (HR 0.959, 95% CI 0.869-1.058; P=0.404), whereas Class 2 and Class 3 remained associated with higher risk relative to Class 1 (Class 2: HR 1.589, 95% CI 1.029-2.455; P=0.037; Class 3: HR 1.620, 95% CI 1.079-2.432; P=0.020).

table.header: Independent Contributions of Trajectory Class and Cumulative Average eGDR
table.expanded: In ELSA, cumulative average eGDR was likewise not independently associated with incident CVD (HR 0.978, 95% CI 0.849-1.127; P=0.760), and the estimates for Class 2 and Class 3 remained directionally consistent with those in HRS, although with wider confidence intervals and without statistical significance.

table.expanded: A linear association between annual eGDR change and incident CVD was observed in HRS (overall P=0.002; nonlinearity P=0.507), whereas no statistically significant association was detected in ELSA (overall P=0.271; nonlinearity P=0.871).

table.header: Independent Contributions of Trajectory Class and Cumulative Average eGDR
table.expanded: In HRS, cumulative average eGDR was no longer associated with incident CVD after adjustment for trajectory class (HR 0.959, 95% CI 0.869-1.058; P=0.404), whereas Class 2 and Class 3 remained associated with higher risk relative to Class 1 (Class 2: HR 1.589, 95% CI 1.029-2.455; P=0.037; Class 3: HR 1.620, 95% CI 1.079-2.432; P=0.020).

table.header: Independent Contributions of Trajectory Class and Cumulative Average eGDR
table.expanded: In ELSA, cumulative average eGDR was likewise not independently associated with incident CVD (HR 0.978, 95% CI 0.849-1.127; P=0.760), and the estimates for Class 2 and Class 3 remained directionally consistent with those in HRS, although with wider confidence intervals and without statistical significance.

table.header: Independent Contributions of Trajectory Class and Cumulative Average eGDR
table.expanded: Likelihood ratio tests further showed that, in HRS, adding trajectory class significantly improved model fit beyond cumulative average eGDR alone (P=0.011), whereas adding cumulative average eGDR to the trajectory model did not (P=0.402).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.
